questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique and when do you use it?
questions.title: The Two-Pointer Technique
questions.direct_answer: Two pointers uses two indices into an array to solve in O(n) time and O(1) space. The common forms: opposite ends (lo at 0, hi at end; move them toward the middle — pair sum on a sorted array, reverse in place), fast/slow (fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1 — find a cycle or middle), and parallel (both move forward — merge two sorted arrays). It works when the array is sorted or the problem has a natural left-right structure, turning an O(n^2) nested loop into one O(n) pass. You move a pointer based on the comparison (if sum is too small, move lo up; too big, move hi down).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the forms (opposite ends, fast/slow, parallel) and that it turns O(n^2) nested loops into O(n) with O(1) space.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using two pointers on an unsorted array for pair sum (sort first), or moving the wrong pointer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Two pointers: two indices, O(n) time, O(1) space. Forms: opposite ends (pair sum, reverse), fast/slow (cycle, middle), parallel (merge). Needs sorted or left-right structure.

sections.title: Two-Pointer Forms
sections.content:
Opposite ends, fast/slow, parallel — each O(n) time, O(1) space.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Opposite ends: lo+hi -> middle] --> P[pair sum, reverse]
  F[Fast/slow: 2x and 1x] --> C[cycle, middle]
  PA[Parallel: both forward] --> M[merge sorted]
```

sections.title: Two pointers
sections.content:
```ruby
# Opposite ends: pair sum on a SORTED array
def pair_sum(nums, target)
  lo, hi = 0, nums.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    return [nums[lo], nums[hi]] if s == target
    s < target ? lo += 1 : hi -= 1     # too small -> lo up; too big -> hi down
  end
  nil
end

# Opposite ends: reverse in place
def reverse!(arr)
  lo, hi = 0, arr.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    arr[lo], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[lo]
    lo += 1; hi -= 1
  end
  arr
end

# Fast/slow: find the middle of a linked list (or a cycle)
# slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using two pointers for pair sum on an UNSORTED array (sort it first, or use a hash).
Moving the wrong pointer (too small -> lo up; too big -> hi down — not the reverse).
Forgetting it needs O(1) extra space is the point (don't add a hash unnecessarily).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Two pointers uses two indices; O(n) time, O(1) space — turns O(n^2) into one pass.
Opposite ends (lo+hi -> middle): pair sum on a sorted array, reverse in place.
Fast/slow (2x and 1x): find a cycle or the middle.
Parallel (both forward): merge two sorted arrays.
It needs a sorted array or a natural left-right structure (sort first for pair sum).
